segments.say: Lesson 13. Reliability: Retries, Circuit Breakers & S L Os. Timeouts, exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, redundancy, and S L Is/S L Os/error budgets.

Reliability means the system keeps working when parts fail: timeouts, smart retries, circuit breakers and redundancy contain failures, and S L Os define "working". Here is an analogy. A building's fuses and fire doors: when one circuit fails, the fuse cuts it off so the whole building doesn't go dark.

Why does this matter? "What happens if X fails?" is asked in every design round. A few key words. Timeout: Give up waiting after N ms. Retry with backoff: Try again, waiting longer each time. Circuit breaker: Stop calling a failing service for a while. S L O: Internal reliability target (for example 99.9%). Error budget: Allowed failure: 100% minus S L O.
Circuit breaker states. Closed: normal operation. The breaker counts failures from the downstream service (say, Payments).
Failures exceed a threshold leads to trip open. Calls fail immediately (or use a fallback) instead of waiting on timeouts, which protects threads and the struggling service.
After a cool-down, go half-open: allow a few trial requests.
Trials succeed leads to close again. Normal traffic resumes.
Trials fail leads to back to open. This stops cascading failures, where one slow dependency exhausts every caller's resources.
Exponential backoff with jitter. Retry immediately and you hammer a struggling service. Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt.
But if 10k clients failed at the same moment, they all retry in sync: a thundering herd at 1 s, 2 s, 4 s.
Jitter: randomize each delay (for example random between 0 and 2^n). Retries spread out and the service can recover.
Always pair retries with timeouts, a max attempt count, idempotency, and a retry budget, so retries don't amplify an outage.

Resilience toolkit. Timeouts everywhere (no infinite waits). Retries with exponential backoff plus jitter, only for transient errors and idempotent ops. Circuit breakers to fail fast on unhealthy dependencies. Bulkheads: isolate resource pools so one slow dependency can't sink everything. Fallbacks / graceful degradation: cached data, default recommendations, a "try later" queue. Redundancy: multiple instances, A Zs and regions. Avoid single points of failure. Load shedding & rate limiting to protect yourself under overload.

S L I / S L O / S L A. S L I (indicator): a measured metric, for example % of requests under 300 ms, success rate. S L O (objective): internal target, for example 99.9% success over 30 days. S L A (agreement): contractual promise with penalties, looser than the S L O. Error budget equals 100% minus S L O. 99.9% allows ~43 min of downtime a month. Spend it on releases; freeze risky changes when it's exhausted.

Availability math. 99.9% about 8.8 h/year. 99.99% about 53 min/year. Services in series multiply (0.999 times 0.999 about 99.8%); redundant parallel copies improve availability: 1 minus (0.01)² equals 99.99%.

Say it in the interview. "Every remote call gets a timeout, bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter for idempotent operations, and a circuit breaker with a fallback. I'd isolate critical paths with bulkheads, run across availability zones, and define S L Is/S L Os with error budgets that drive alerting and release decisions.".

Let's compare. Timeout: threads stuck forever, 2 s on payment call. Retry plus backoff plus jitter: transient failures; herds, 3 tries: ~1 s, ~2 s, ~4 s randomized. Circuit breaker: cascading failures, stop calling failing recommender. Bulkhead: resource exhaustion spreading, separate thread pool per dependency. Fallback: hard failures for users, show cached prices. Load shedding: total collapse under overload, drop low-priority requests (503).

A likely interview question: How do you stop one slow service from taking down everything? A strong answer: Timeouts, a circuit breaker with fallback, bulkheaded resource pools, bounded retries with jittered backoff, and load shedding, plus alerting on S L O burn rate.
That's it for Reliability: Retries, Circuit Breakers & S L Os. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
